figures.caption: Fig. 1 The Platonic brain bridge: forward link, reverse link and one sparse feature set. a, Forward link (model to brain). Ridge read-outs map hidden states of seven omni models to 1,000 cortical parcels in four participants watching Friends. Shown are encoding r for Ming-flash-omni-2.0 (four views); the five Algonauts 2025 leaderboard columns (orange, this pool; grey, best other entry); a sagittal Yeo-7 section with its colour key; network-level r̄ per model; the brain-likeness spectrum (rank agreement ρ = 0.958); and r̄ of three bases under six input subsets. b, Reverse link (brain to model). The Yeo-7 networks map onto seven LoRA experts BkAk (lock, Ak frozen after stage one); a read-only side-probe supplies the brain prior pbrain to the gate (symbols in Methods), and the gated experts add residually to the frozen base. Heat map, held-out gain ∆1 over that base (pp; three bases × five benchmarks); forest plot, ∆2 (brain minus capacity-matched random experts) with 95% McNemar intervals (filled, Holm-significant; pale, uncorrected; open, n.s.; shape, base). c, Brain-Scope in three roles: read out, inject pbrain, ablate (zbrain ← 0). Bars, from left: the routing hit rate, the share of held-out questions whose top-weighted expert is the annotated network, divided by the independence baseline (dashed line at 1; two splits per base, P < 2× 10−4); paired |r| of matched brain-aligned features against the best circular shift (P = 1/12,045); and excess damage in r̄ from zeroing them against energy-matched controls (n = 709 parcels), which also costs 9.6 pp of OmniBench accuracy on Qwen3-Omni.

Fig. 3 Modality structure, depth structure and the capability-brain-likeness relation. a, Whole-cortex brainlikeness of three base models (Ming-flash-omni-2.0, circles; MiniCPM-o 4.5, squares; Qwen3-Omni, diamonds) under six input-modality subsets (T text, V video, A audio and combinations); all three follow T < V < {A, V+T} < V+A < V+A+T; error bars, 95% confidence intervals (paired parcel bootstrap, 10,000 resamples, n = 1,000 parcels); A and V+T overlap in MiniCPM-o 4.5 and Qwen3-Omni. b, Marginal gain of one added channel between nested subsets; audio and subtitles each add less in a richer context, and all 27 nested comparisons raise brain-likeness. c, Increment of full-modality over video-only input decomposed by Yeo-7 network (network colours; within each network, left to right, Ming, MiniCPM, Qwen3). d, Single-layer brain-likeness of seven models at four relative depths (1/4, 2/4, 3/4, last); triangles mark the peak of each model; 0/7 models peak at the last layer. e, Peak relative depth against a capability composite (mean z-score over WorldSense, Daily-Omni and MMAU); Spearman ρ = +0.40, exhaustive permutation P = 0.43, n = 7. f, Last-to-peak brain-likeness ratio against the capability composite; ρ = −0.786, P = 0.048, n = 7; no correlation on this seven-model panel remains significant after Holm correction over the family of six (smallest corrected P = 0.29); the partial Pearson coefficient in h is outside that family. g, Capability composite against whole-cortex r̄; zero-order Pearson r = +0.29, exhaustive label permutation (5,040) P = 0.54. h, Partial Spearman, partial Pearson (controlling log10 parameters) and zero-order Pearson coefficients on all seven models (dark grey) and on six models without Ming-flash-omni-2.0 (light grey). i, Composition of the capability composite: accuracy z-scores of the seven models on the three benchmarks (raw accuracies in cells). In e to g, grey lines are least-squares fits and shading is the bootstrap 95% confidence band (2,000 resamples); point colours follow d.

Fig. 4 Brain-aligned sparse features converge across models, whereas inter-model differences concentrate on one low-dimensional shared axis. a, Mean activation-series correlation |r| after one-to-one Hungarian matching of the brain-aligned sparse features of each model (185, 184 and 190 for Qwen3-Omni, Ming-flash-omni-2.0 and MiniCPM-o 4.5) over 13,383 shared stimulus grid points for three pairs of independently trained models (orange) against the largest matched correlation reached by any circular shift of one series (grey, the permutation null maximum); ratios in parentheses; exact circular-shift permutation P = 1/12,045 per pair. b, Variance spectrum of the inter-model residual matrix, the seven Schaefer-1000 encoding maps with the shared map removed; participation ratio 1.28 out of 6 possible dimensions. c, Robustness of the effective dimension to five treatments addressing four alternative explanations (orange points); dashed line, observed value; independent noise at the measured residual amplitude (2,000 simulations) lies outside the axis range and is annotated as text. d, Mean loading of the first residual principal component on the Yeo-7 networks (bar colours, network colours; parcel counts above bars); sensory and attention networks (orange background) against association networks (blue background). e, Relabelling null (all 7! = 5,040 label permutations) of |Spearman ρ| between the capability-brain coupling map and PC1; orange line, observed value; dashed line, null median. f, Cortical distribution of PC1 loadings (glass-brain projection, four views; diverging colour scale centred at zero). g, Distribution over 1,000 parcels of the coupling between the capability composite and parcel-wise brain-likeness: orange, partial correlation controlling parameter count; blue, zero-order; vertical lines, mean and median. h, Exact permutation null of the mean coupling under all 5,040 model relabellings; orange line, observed value (two-sided P = 0.55). i, The same parcel-wise partial correlations grouped by Yeo-7 network. Each violin is the distribution over the parcels of one network, with individual parcels as jittered points; the white dot marks the median and the bar the mean. The numbers above each violin give the fraction of parcels with a positive correlation, the numbers below give the network mean, and the parcel count of each network is given on the x axis.

Fig. 5 Forward data flow of Brain-MoE, two-stage training, the Brain-Scope loop and learned gating weights. a, Forward computation at one injection point (attention projections of layers 20 to 28 for MiniCPM-o 4.5 and Ming-flashomni-2.0, and of layers 28 to 36 for Qwen3-Omni). The hidden state h takes two paths: the expert path (purple) with seven brain-feature experts BkAkh (Yeo-7 colours; Ak frozen after stage one, lock icon; Bk trained in stage two), and the read-only sparse-autoencoder bypass (green), which passes the probe-layer state through the TopK sparse autoencoder, the brain readout R and Yeo-7 pooling to give pbrain, which enters the gate through the topology operator Π (real, rotate, uniform; red dashed box) with one learnable gain per network; the expert outputs are weighted by g and added residually to the frozen base projection. b, Two-stage training. Stage one trains Ak network by network with a GDPO-inspired REINFORCE variant on Brain-AVQA and merges the seven experts; stage two freezes Ak (lock) and trains Bk and the gate (flame) on the training split of each benchmark; brain and random arms share architecture, steps and data. c, The two directions of one sparse autoencoder: Brain-Scope (TopK-SAE and readout R, fitted from human fMRI) reads out brain responses in the forward chain and aggregates predicted responses into pbrain in the reverse chain, with identical parameters and no answer-loss gradient in either direction. d, Gating weights learned by the brain arm on held-out questions of five public benchmarks: mean weight gk of the seven experts in 15 model and benchmark combinations (stacks normalized per cell; no error bars). e, The same gating weights as a heat map, with the seven networks as rows and the 15 cells as columns.

Fig. 6 Two levels of evidence on three heterogeneous bases and five public benchmarks. a, Heat maps of held-out accuracy gains in pp: left, gain ∆1 of the brain-pretrained expert arm over the frozen base; middle, gain of the capacity-matched random expert arm over the same base (shared 0 to 12 scale); right, their difference ∆2 (zero-centred diverging scale). Stars, per-question paired exact McNemar tests (left and middle, arm versus base; right, brain versus random; *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001; bracketed stars, P < 0.05 that fails Holm correction over 15 cells; exact per-cell P values of the brain-versus-random comparison are listed in Extended Data Table 5). Columns, OmniBench, MMAU, MMAU-Pro, MuChoMusic, MUSIC-AVQA v2.0 (held-out n = 571, 490, 2,203, 425, 179); rows, Ming-flash-omni-2.0, MiniCPM-o 4.5, Qwen3-Omni. b, Forest plot of ∆2 in the 15 cells grouped by base (dark red circles, Ming-flash-omni-2.0; gold squares, MiniCPM-o 4.5; blue triangles, Qwen3-Omni); bars, 95% confidence intervals from discordant pairs; filled, significant after Holm correction; filled with inner dot, uncorrected significance only; open, P ≥ 0.05; the sub-axis on the right gives the numbers of questions answered correctly only by the brain arm (orange) and only by the random arm (purple). c, Null distributions of the question-level joint sign-flip permutation (Nperm = 100,000; one sign per question shared across the three bases): left, number of cells with ∆2 > 0 (observed 14, right tail shaded); right, kernel density of the mean ∆2 over 15 cells (observed value marked). d, Fraction of held-out questions per cell answered correctly only by the brain arm (orange, upward) and only by the random arm (purple, downward); background shading groups bases.

Excess damage was +9.11 pp over the matched control (paired exact test, P = 7.3×10−7, n = 571) and +1.73 pp pooled over five benchmarks (n = 3,868, P = 0.0041) (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g). Ming and MiniCPM showed near-zero downstream excess damage, whereas Qwen3 also showed the largest encoding excess damage, so on that base benchmark accuracy depends on its brain-aligned features.
